<reason>Both sides were competent and produced a genuine comparative debate, but Side A (CON) edged it on execution and clash resolution. A's core frame — the retirement age is a "gate" that cannot be aimed, while payroll contributions are a "dial" that can be tilted toward higher earnings and a broader base — persisted across every round and was never squarely broken. B's best counters (the empathy reversal in B2.2, the treadmill framing, the gift-generations argument) were strong and original, and B answered pressure questions honestly, but B's admission that the statutory default must track the national mean conceded the heart of A's inequality critique, and B's "targeted calibration" fix relies on the same political machinery B criticized as optimistic on CON's side. A's answer to the double-standard pressure (a cap is an existing parameter; carve-outs are categorically underinclusive because worn-out is not disabled) drew a real distinction B never fully dissolved. B also suffered two clipped turns (opening and Rebuttal 1), a real execution cost, and B's closing claimed A "never answered" the progressivity point when A had answered it repeatedly. A's speeches were tighter, answered pressure directly with required A1/A2 labels, and crystallized cleanly without new material.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The decisive exchange was B's pressure question on the political double standard (B3.2) versus A's Rebuttal 2 answer (A4.3): A distinguished cap-lifts as existing parameters that change who pays from carve-outs that miss worn-out-but-not-disabled workers by design, then weaponized B's own concession that the default tracks the national mean — "Targeted relief admits the mean is the wrong ruler—then keeps using it as the default." That exchange left B's fairness calibration looking under-defended against A's un-aimable-gate frame.</best_rebuttal>
